abstract: While rare in nature, fluorinated compounds are ubiquitous in synthetic chemicals ranging from pharmaceuticals to agrochemicals, yet how proteins recognize these anthropogenic molecules remains poorly understood. Here, we use three structurally and evolutionarily divergent solute-binding proteins (SBPs) specific for short-chain dicarboxylic acids as a comparative model system to dissect the principles governing protein-fluorocompound recognition. X-ray crystal structures reveal that each SBP uses a distinct binding mode, ranging from backbone-mediated to side-chain-dominated hydrogen bonding. Despite their structural divergence, ITC shows that all three proteins exhibit a conserved vulnerability upon binding perfluorinated ligands: binding affinity drops up to 80-fold, or is abolished, across all three proteins regardless of fold or binding mode. In contrast, sensitivity to partial fluorination is locally tunable, with one protein even binding a fluorinated ligand more tightly than its non-fluorinated counterpart. Using X-ray crystallography, molecular dynamics simulations, and site-directed mutagenesis, we show that aromatic residues positioned near the ligand contribute to this tunability, capable of either penalizing or favoring fluorinated ligands. Together, these findings establish that ligand-fluorination sensitivity reflects a conserved chemical vulnerability layered with locally tunable, structurally encoded selectivity, providing a roadmap for predicting and engineering protein recognition of fluorinated compounds.
